content: 1. In regions with a low prevalence of HCV infection, no definitive confirmatory test has been developed. However, supplemental tests, such as the licensed Recombinant Immunoblot Assay, are available and should always be used to confirm repeatedly reactive results obtained from screening assays. 2. The diagnosis of HCV infection can also be achieved by detecting HCV RNA using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) techniques. 3. Although PCR assays for HCV RNA are commercially available for research purposes, the results can vary significantly between laboratories. 4. In a recent study involving a reference panel containing known HCV RNA-positive and -negative sera provided to 86 laboratories worldwide, only 50% of the laboratories performed adequately, with some failing to detect a weak positive sample. Only 16% of the laboratories reported flawless results. 5. False-positive and false-negative results can occur due to improper collection, handling, and storage of test samples. 6. Additionally, because HCV RNA may only be intermittently detectable during the course of infection, a single negative PCR test result should not be considered conclusive. 7. Tests have been developed to quantify HCV RNA in serum; however, their clinical applicability has not been determined. 8. 9. The prevalence of anti-HCV among hospital-based HCWs and surgeons is approximately 1%, while it is about 2% among oral surgeons. 10.8%, with a range of 0% to 7%. 11. 12. 13. Several studies have examined the effectiveness of prophylaxis with immune globulins (IGs) in preventing post-transfusion non-A, non-B hepatitis. However, the findings are difficult to compare and interpret due to variability in diagnostic criteria, mixed donor sources, and differing study designs. 14. In some studies, IGs appeared to reduce the rate of clinical disease but not the overall infection rates. 15. In one study, data suggested that chronic hepatitis was less likely to develop in patients who received IG. 16. None of these data have been reanalyzed since anti-HCV testing became available. 17. 18. 19. Furthermore, IG is now manufactured from plasma that has been screened for anti-HCV. 20. 21. The prevention of HCV infection with antiviral agents, such as alpha interferon, has not been studied. 22. Although alpha interferon therapy is safe and effective for the treatment of chronic hepatitis C, the mechanisms of its effect are poorly understood. 23. Interferon may only be effective in the presence of an established infection. 24. Interferon must be administered by injection and may cause side effects. 25. 26. In the absence of effective prophylaxis, individuals who have been exposed to HCV may benefit from knowing their infection status so they can seek evaluation for chronic liver disease and treatment. 27. Sustained response rates to alpha interferon therapy are generally low, ranging from 10% to 20% in the United States. 28. The occurrence of mild to moderate side effects in most patients has required discontinuation of therapy in up to 15% of patients. 29. No clinical, demographic, serum biochemical, serologic, or histologic features have been identified that reliably predict which patients will sustain a long-term remission in response to alpha interferon therapy. 30. Several studies indicate that interferon treatment initiated early in the course of HCV infection is associated with an increased rate of resolved infection. 31. 32. However, PCR is not a licensed assay, and its accuracy is highly variable. 33. Additionally, no data are available to indicate that treatment initiated early in the course of chronic HCV infection is less effective than treatment begun during the acute phase of infection. 34. Furthermore, alpha interferon is approved only for the treatment of chronic hepatitis C. 35. 36. No vaccine against hepatitis C is available. 37. 38. At a minimum, such policies should include baseline serologic testing for anti-HCV for the source, baseline and follow-up (e.g., 6 months) serologic testing for anti-HCV and alanine aminotransferase activity for the exposed person, confirmation of all anti-HCV results reported as repeatedly reactive by EIA using supplemental anti-HCV testing, and education of HCWs about the risk for and prevention of occupational transmission of all bloodborne pathogens, including hepatitis C, using up-to-date and accurate information.
